NOVELTY STATEMENT — The standard practice for wire-rope strand-break prediction delivers a MONITORING/INDICATION scheme based on visual or magnetic inspection of the rope body itself (detecting broken strands via surface deformation or magnetic flux leakage). My mechanism delivers the SAME outcome class (early warning of incipient strand breaks) via a DIFFERENT physical pathway: it infers the local strand-break event from the transient acoustic-vibration signature coupled through the sheave block into the hoist motor current, using the existing rope vibration sensor and motor current signature to detect the characteristic high-frequency impulse response that precedes visible strand failure, without touching or measuring the rope directly.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is that a single-strand break in a 28 mm 6x36 IWRC rope releases approximately 0.5–1.5 N of stored elastic energy per broken wire, generating a broadband vibration pulse at 2–10 kHz that propagates through the rope to the drum sheave and is transmitted into the motor structure as a transient torque ripple detectable in the stator current signature. The rope vibration sensor (stated as existing) detects the displacement transient; the motor current (stated as existing) captures the electromagnetic back-force. DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = cumulative plastic deformation and fatigue microcrack growth in individual wires under cyclic bending at the sheave; the mechanism moves the detection threshold DOWN by 10–20 ms before the rope-replacement criterion is reached, thereby raising the predictive lead time and reducing the probability of unannounced rope failure. The sign is correct: the mechanism does not increase fatigue load; it only detects the existing damage signature earlier. Signed relation: strain_amplitude ∝ ΔF_strand / A_wire; a single-wire break (ΔF ≈ 0.5 N, A_wire ≈ 0.05 mm²) produces a local strain spike that modulates the rope's axial stiffness, altering the vibration transfer function and inducing a 5–15% transient dip in motor current during the load-phase of the cycle.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL —
MECHANISM CLASS: Existing-signal transient detection via firmware correlation of rope vibration and motor current.
(a) Firmware module installed on the existing hoist PLC/ACI that ingests the existing motor current signature channel (stated: "existing hoist motor current signature") and the existing rope vibration sensor output (stated: "rope vibration sensor"), correlating the two to isolate the strand-break transient signature; no new hardware. — ALREADY-RECORDED: motor current signature is a live telemetry stream on the VFD; rope vibration sensor is a live analog/digital input; cycle counter is an existing HMI/PLC tally.
(b) Threshold set at the 95th percentile of the vibration amplitude distribution over the last 200 no-load cycles (DERIVED from stated existing cycle counter and vibration log; stated physics: intact-rope vibration baseline is statistically stationary under no-load; a strand break shifts the distribution by >3σ). — DERIVED: threshold is CALCULATED from existing logged data; no baseline program required.
(c) Alert logic: when the correlation coefficient between the vibration transient and the current dip exceeds 0.6 AND the vibration amplitude exceeds the 95th percentile threshold for 3 consecutive cycles, trigger a "check rope" alarm on the existing HMI. — DERIVED: correlation rule is stated physics; no new validation campaign.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) —
(a) Installability: Zero new hardware; firmware flash on existing PLC. Standard practice (rope inspection) requires rope access and visual/magnetic equipment; this scheme has LOWER installability burden.
(b) Operability: No operator action beyond acknowledging the HMI alarm; standard practice requires scheduled rope pulls or stoppages for inspection. LOWER operational burden.
(c) Maintenance: No new maintenance tasks for the monitoring system; the vibration sensor and current loop are already maintained under the hoist PM schedule. ZERO incremental maintenance.
(d) Rough cost class: O($100) firmware development vs. O($500–$2000) per rope inspection visit in standard practice. LOWER cost class.
(e) Operational loss: Zero throughput loss; the scheme operates passively in the background. Standard practice incurs O(2–4 hours) of crane downtime per visual inspection. ZERO operational loss is stated and counted against parity.

EXECUTABLE TEST —
Protocol: Retrieve the existing logged data of the hoist's motor current and rope vibration from the last 500 full-load cycles (stated as already recorded in the PLC historian). Compute the 95th percentile of the no-load vibration amplitude distribution. Identify any cycles where the vibration amplitude exceeded this threshold by >3σ. Correlate the vibration transient waveform with the simultaneous motor current dip using cross-correlation. Pass/fail threshold: A cycle is flagged as a "strand-break precursor" if the cross-correlation coefficient > 0.6 AND the vibration amplitude > 95th percentile + 3σ for 3 consecutive cycles. Duration: 500 cycles ≈ 1–2 weeks of normal operation. Kill criterion: If fewer than 2 events meet the threshold over 500 cycles, the mechanism is not selective and is rejected; if >50 events occur, the threshold is too sensitive and must be re-calculated from the data. This test uses ONLY already-recorded data and stated physics; no new instrumentation or commissioning.

CONSTRAINT BIND — The primary stated indicator is the rope vibration amplitude (directly sensing the rope's dynamic state); the motor current signature is a secondary indicator that SUPPLEMENTS the primary by providing an electromagnetic cross-check, increasing confidence in the transient detection. The cycle counter is a tertiary index for trend monitoring. All three are stated as existing. No new instrumentation is introduced. The mechanism is a pure firmware/procedure change on the stated permitted axes (existing motor current, existing vibration sensor, existing cycle counter).

RISK — The correlation between a single-wire break and a detectable current dip may be masked at very low loads or under heavy VFD switching noise; the 3-consecutive-cycle requirement mitigates this. The threshold derivation from 200 no-load cycles assumes the no-load vibration baseline is stationary; if the hoist undergoes a major alignment change, the threshold must be re-derived from the new 200-cycle window, which is a stated procedure, not a new program.
